eligibility.evidence: Methods p.23-25, Table 1/3: GPT-4 estimates the probability and ambiguity of 23 verbal probability phrases (taken from O'Brien 1989) in two contexts, alongside 50 humans. E2 met via the verbal-probability interpretation literature the paper cites; borderline because it is a coordination-game framing rather than a named classic paradigm.

A.title: Use of probabilistic phrases in a coordination game: human versus GPT-4

paradigms.name: Probability estimation for verbal probability phrases (decoding stage of a coordination game), investment and medical contexts
Ambiguity (imprecision) rating of verbal probability phrases, investment and medical contexts

D.population: NYU SONA subject-pool students, 25 per context (between-participants), mostly aged 18-35
D.metric: median human rating per phrase; linear fit (slope, intercept) of human median on GPT-4; discordance

effects.label: AGREEMENT-ONLY
effects.location: Results 1A, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, p.10-13: discordance of GPT-4 below human median in both contexts; slope of human on GPT-4 0.833 (Investment) and 0.825 (Medical), both significantly below 1; no correlation coefficient reported. Pooled over the two contexts as the authors report them separately (both given).

effects.label: AGREEMENT-ONLY
effects.location: Results 1B, Fig. 4, p.13-14: slope of human on GPT-4 0.530 (Investment) and 0.710 (Medical), both significantly below 1; discordance not analysed for ambiguity; no correlation coefficient reported.

E.headline: GPT-4 agreed with humans on probability at least as well as humans agreed with each other, but human estimates were compressed relative to GPT-4; ambiguity differed more.

G.notes: Main analyses use one GPT-4 run; only the Medical probability task was rerun four times (Fig. 7, p.17-18), so stability is shown for one cell. Two outliers removed from main-text tests. Model version, date and temperature unreported (chat interface). Context effect (null for probability, present for ambiguity) is not coded as a separate row.
